concept.shortExplanation: Attention and feed-forward blocks are not the only reason transformers work — the plumbing around them is doing real load-bearing work. A residual connection adds each block's input back to its output, so the block only has to learn a correction and gradients get an unobstructed path back to earlier layers. Layer normalisation rescales each token's activations to a consistent statistic, which stops the values drifting as depth accumulates. Remove either one and deep stacks stop training. The activation traces here are real hidden states pulled from every layer of a live model.
concept.ahaMoment: Depth was never blocked by a lack of ideas about what layers should compute. It was blocked by numbers drifting and gradients dying, and two pieces of plumbing fixed both.

modelRequirement.loadFailureMessage: The transformer could not be downloaded, so per-layer hidden states cannot be read. Check your connection and retry — it works offline once cached.

levels.title: Trace the Norms
levels.instructions: Real hidden-state magnitudes, layer by layer, extracted from the model. Predict how the activation norm evolves with depth before revealing the measured trace.

engineConfig.sentence: the engineer reviewed the schematic before signing off on the design

hints: This trace has both the residual path and layer norm on — the same combination every real trained transformer ships with. Think about what layer norm's job actually is before guessing how much the numbers move.
Layer norm rescales every token's activations to a consistent statistic at every single layer, so with it on the trace should barely move across depth at all — not grow, not shrink.

For this sentence, the measured L2 norm sits at essentially 19.6 at every one of the 7 layers (the embedding output included) — that's sqrt(384), the model's hidden size, which is exactly what a properly layer-normalised representation should measure. Guess about 19.6 for every round.

levels.title: Pull the Plumbing
levels.instructions: Toggle the residual path and layer norm off and recompute the stack from the model's real per-layer states. Find the configuration where activations stay in a stable band across all layers.

engineConfig.sentence: the engineer reviewed the schematic before signing off on the design

hints: Start by looking at the number with both mechanisms off — it's as unstable as this stack gets. Then flip them on one at a time and watch which one actually pulls it into a tight band.

Residual alone (layer norm still off) helps, but doesn't fully fix it — the activation magnitude can still swing across layers even when each block's input carries forward. Layer norm is what forces every layer's magnitude back to the same statistic, on its own or combined with the residual path.

With both off, only 3 of 7 layers land inside the stable band (0.43 — well under the pass mark). Residual alone reaches 6 of 7 (0.857, 2 stars). Turning layer norm on — with or without the residual path — puts all 7 layers in band for a perfect 1.0.

levels.title: Minimise the Drift
levels.instructions: Deeper stack, your own sentence. Tune the residual scale and normalisation epsilon to keep drift between consecutive layers as low as possible without flattening the representation entirely.

engineConfig.sentence: the engineer reviewed the schematic before signing off on the design

hints: The starting normalisation epsilon is much larger than any real transformer would use — that's exactly what's driving the drift up. Try dragging it down, a couple of orders of magnitude at a time.

Don't chase a lower number by dragging the residual scale toward zero. Collapsing the representation to near-nothing is measured and penalised separately from drift, and that penalty is far larger than any drift you'd save.

On the shipped sentence, the starting epsilon of 2 gives drift ≈ 0.097 — already failing. Epsilon 0.01 brings it to ≈ 0.006 (2 stars). Epsilon 0.00001, a realistic value for a real transformer, brings it to ≈ 0.000007 — a clean 3 stars. Leave the residual scale at 1.
